name: Words Worth Knowing
description: Uncommon English words caught in the wild, one card each: see the word, say what it means. Extras carry the etymology and the near-miss word each one gets confused with (furor is not fervor, stupor is not torpor). A deck built to grow as new words turn up.

fields.back: An outbreak of public anger or excitement over something.
fields.extra: From Latin *furor*, 'rage', from *furere*, 'to rage'. Not *fervor*, which is from *fervere*, 'to boil' - heat inside one person, where a furor is noise outside among many. British English spells it *furore* and says it in three syllables (fyoo-ROR-ee).

fields.back: A state of near-unconsciousness in which someone barely responds to anything around them.
fields.extra: From Latin *stupere*, 'to be stunned' - the same root behind *stupid* and *stupendous*. Not *torpor*, which is dulled activity rather than dulled awareness: torpor fits an animal in winter dormancy, stupor fits a mind that will not come back to the surface.

From Latin *beatus*, 'blessed, happy'. Capitalized, the Beatitudes are the blessings Jesus pronounces at the opening of the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:3-12, each line beginning 'Blessed are'). Not *beatification*, which is the Church declaring a dead person 'Blessed' on the way to sainthood.

fields.back: Painstaking care to get things both exactly right and morally right.
fields.extra: From Latin *scrupulus*, 'a small sharp stone' - the pebble in the shoe of the conscience, which is why the word covers precision and principle at once. *Meticulousness* is only the precision half. Note also *scrupulosity*, the clinical term for guilt over moral or religious failings taken to a pathological extreme.
